titleEn: Do not burn with anger at evildoers
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Forty verses of advice for one problem: the wicked are doing well and you are not. This is a wisdom poem, closer to Proverbs than to a prayer, and it argues rather than pleads. It is built as an alphabetical acrostic, but not a tidy one: most letters open a two-verse strophe, so the letter changes roughly every other verse, while dalet at verse 7, kaf at verse 20 and qof at verse 34 get one verse each, samekh at verse 27 stretches over three, and no verse in the Masoretic text begins with ayin. A learner should track one phrase: inheriting the land, which comes back at verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34 and is the psalm's answer each time. Verse 25 is the one most people know, because it is said at the table in the Grace after Meals.

stichs.en: Of David.
Do not burn with anger at evildoers,
do not envy those who do wrong.

verses.summary: The psalm opens on a prohibition, not a complaint. The problem it treats is not the evildoer but what the sight of him does to the person watching.

stichs.en: For like grass they wither quickly,
and fade like green shoots.

verses.summary: The reason given is duration, not justice. Grass in this climate is the standard image for something that is genuinely green and genuinely brief.

stichs.en: Trust in the LORD and do good,
dwell in the land and feed on faithfulness.

verses.summary: Four imperatives, and only the first is inward. The counsel is not to feel differently but to stay put and keep working.

stichs.en: And take your delight in the LORD,
and He will give you what your heart asks.

verses.summary: The verb for delight is reflexive: you do it to yourself. The promise follows the practice rather than replacing it.

stichs.en: Roll your way onto the LORD,
trust in Him, and He will act.

verses.summary: A physical verb: you roll a load off yourself onto something that can carry it. The final clause has no object, which is part of its force.

stichs.en: He will bring your righteousness out like the light,
and your case like noon.

verses.summary: The vindication is public and visible. Noon is chosen because it is the hour with no shadow to hide anything.

stichs.en: Be silent before the LORD and wait for Him.
Do not burn at the man who makes his way prosper,
at a man who carries out his schemes.

verses.summary: The prohibition of verse 1 returns, and the target is sharpened: not evil in general but the specific man whose plans are working.

stichs.en: Let go of anger and leave rage behind;
do not burn, it leads only to harm.

verses.summary: The third and last time the verb appears, now with the consequence stated: resentment does not stay a feeling, it turns into an act.

stichs.en: For evildoers will be cut off,
but those who wait for the LORD, they will inherit the land.

verses.summary: First appearance of the refrain. The pronoun before the verb is emphatic: these and not the others are the ones who stay.

stichs.en: A little longer, and the wicked man is gone;
you will look at his place, and he is not there.

verses.summary: The disappearance is described from the observer's side. You are still standing there; it is the place that has emptied.

stichs.en: But the humble will inherit the land,
and take delight in abundant peace.

verses.summary: The refrain returns with a new subject. The same reflexive verb of delight used of God in verse 4 is now used of peace.

stichs.en: The wicked man plots against the righteous,
and grinds his teeth at him.

verses.summary: A block of five verses on the threat begins here. The psalm does not deny the danger; it dates it.

stichs.en: The Lord laughs at him,
for He sees that his day is coming.

verses.summary: The laughter is not mockery of suffering but the reaction of someone who can already see the end of the scene.

stichs.en: The wicked have drawn the sword and bent their bow,
to bring down the poor and needy,
to slaughter those whose way is straight.

verses.summary: The threat is armed and aimed at the weakest, not at rivals. Two infinitives of purpose carry the whole second half.

stichs.en: Their sword will go into their own heart,
and their bows will be broken.

verses.summary: The weapons of the previous verse turn around, in order. No outside agent is named: the sentence is carried out by the equipment.

stichs.en: Better the little that the righteous has
than the wealth of many wicked men.

verses.summary: A proverb dropped into the argument, in the standard better-than form of Proverbs. It answers the envy of verse 1 with arithmetic.

stichs.en: For the arms of the wicked will be broken,
but the LORD holds up the righteous.

verses.summary: Arm means strength here. The same verb for breaking that fell on the bows in verse 15 now falls on the body.

stichs.en: The LORD knows the days of the blameless,
and their inheritance will last for ever.

verses.summary: Knowing days is a way of saying the span is accounted for. The word for inheritance is the noun behind the refrain's verb.

stichs.en: They will not be put to shame in a bad time,
and in days of famine they will eat their fill.

verses.summary: The promise is deliberately modest: not wealth, but enough during the years when there is not enough.

stichs.en: For the wicked will perish,
and the enemies of the LORD are like the glory of the pastures:
they are used up, they go up in smoke, they are used up.

verses.summary: The verse repeats its last word, which is unusual and probably deliberate. The image behind it is contested; see the remez.

stichs.en: The wicked man borrows and does not repay,
but the righteous is generous and gives.

verses.summary: The contrast moves from violence to money. Righteousness here is measured by what leaves the hand, not by what is believed.

stichs.en: For those He blesses will inherit the land,
and those He curses will be cut off.

verses.summary: The refrain a third time, now with both halves attributed directly to God rather than to the behaviour of the parties.

stichs.en: A man's steps are made firm by the LORD,
and He delights in his way.

verses.summary: The subject shifts from what happens to the wicked to what holds the ordinary walker up. Steps and way are the psalm's working metaphor.

stichs.en: Though he falls he is not thrown down,
for the LORD holds his hand.

verses.summary: Falling is conceded. What is denied is the second verb, the one that means being flung down and left there.

stichs.en: I was young and now I am old,
and I have not seen a righteous man abandoned,
nor his children begging for bread.

verses.summary: The one verse in the psalm spoken as personal testimony, and the one most readers argue with. It claims observation, not doctrine.

stichs.en: All day long he is generous and lends,
and his children become a blessing.

verses.summary: It answers verse 25 in its own terms: the children who do not beg are the children of a man who lent to others.

stichs.en: Turn from evil and do good,
and you will dwell for ever.

verses.summary: The imperatives of verse 3 come back almost word for word, and the reward attached to them has grown from the land to for ever.

stichs.en: For the LORD loves justice
and does not abandon His faithful ones.
They are kept safe for ever,
but the seed of the wicked is cut off.

verses.summary: The longest verse in the psalm, and the place where the acrostic goes missing. It gives the reason under everything said so far.

stichs.en: The righteous will inherit the land,
and live on it for ever.

verses.summary: The refrain a fourth time, and the only one that adds a preposition holding them on the land rather than merely receiving it.

stichs.en: The mouth of the righteous murmurs wisdom,
and his tongue speaks justice.

verses.summary: The verb is the low continuous sound of someone reciting under his breath, the same one used of meditating on the Torah.

stichs.en: The teaching of his God is in his heart;
his steps do not slip.

verses.summary: Interior instruction produces exterior stability. It picks the steps of verse 23 back up and states the mechanism.

stichs.en: The wicked man watches the righteous,
looking for a way to kill him.

verses.summary: The threat returns after twenty verses, in the same grammar as verse 12: participle, subject, target.

stichs.en: The LORD will not leave him in his power,
and will not let him be condemned at his trial.

verses.summary: The scene becomes a courtroom. Both verbs carry the object suffix him, which is why the English needs so many more words.

stichs.en: Wait for the LORD and keep His way,
and He will lift you up to possess the land.
When the wicked are cut off, you will see it.

verses.summary: The refrain a fifth and last time, and the only one addressed to you rather than reported about a group.

stichs.en: I have seen a wicked man, a bully,
spreading out like a green tree in its own soil.

verses.summary: Second personal testimony, matching verse 25 and reversing it: here the speaker says what he did see, not what he did not.

stichs.en: Then he was gone,
I looked for him and he was not found.

verses.summary: The tree of the previous verse is not cut down or argued with. It is simply absent at the next visit, which is the whole point.

stichs.en: Watch the blameless man and look at the upright,
for the man of peace has a future.

verses.summary: The instruction is to redirect attention. After thirty-six verses spent looking at the wicked, look at somebody else.

stichs.en: But those who break faith are destroyed together;
the future of the wicked is cut off.

verses.summary: The same noun that meant a future in verse 37 here means what gets severed. The contrast is built on one word.

stichs.en: The rescue of the righteous comes from the LORD,
their refuge in a time of trouble.

verses.summary: Trouble is granted, not denied. The psalm ends by naming a shelter inside the bad time rather than an escape from it.

stichs.en: The LORD helps them and gets them out;
He gets them out from the wicked and saves them,
because they have taken shelter in Him.

verses.summary: Four verbs in a row, all with the suffix them, and one of them said twice. The last clause gives the only condition in the psalm.

pardes.body: Someone is watching a dishonest man do well and it is eating him. The psalm answers with two moves, repeated in cycles. The first is a prohibition against the feeling itself, stated three times with the same verb, at verses 1, 7 and 8. The second is a time argument: what looks permanent is short, so what looks like an unjust distribution is really an unfinished one. Around this the poem builds a refrain, inheriting the land, at verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34, and each occurrence gives the promise to a different subject, those who wait, the humble, those God blesses, the righteous, and finally you. Nothing here is a prayer. There is no request, no complaint addressed upward, and God is spoken about rather than to for all forty verses. It is an older person giving advice, which is exactly how verse 25 presents it.

The acrostic is the frame and it is worth counting. Each Hebrew letter opens a strophe of two verses, so the letter changes every second verse, but four places break the pattern: dalet gets verse 7 alone, kaf gets verse 20 alone, qof gets verse 34 alone, samekh runs across verses 27 to 29, and no verse in the Masoretic text opens with ayin. The Greek version has an extra clause in verse 28 about wrongdoers being destroyed, and many modern editors retrovert that to a lost Hebrew line beginning with ayin, which would restore the sequence; others take the letter as simply missing. Both are conjectures and the printed Hebrew supports neither. A second crux sits in {{20.6}}, a word that can be read as lambs or as meadows: the older translations give the fat of lambs going up on an altar, the newer ones the splendour of pasture that dries out. The verb of {{5.0}} is worth its own note, because it means to roll a weight, not to entrust a matter.

Verse 25 is recited in the Grace after Meals, and it is the verse of this psalm people have always pushed back on, because plenty of righteous people have in fact gone hungry. The traditional readings do not deny that. One takes the line as testimony, David reporting the limits of one lifetime rather than legislating for all of them. Another reads it forward into verse 26 and makes it conditional: the children who do not beg are the children of a man who spent his own days lending. Both readings agree that a verse about not having seen something is not a verse about it being impossible. The refrain about inheriting the land was heard by later readers as more than a property claim, since {{11.0}}, the humble, are promised the same land that armies were fighting over, and the psalm's own logic is that possession follows patience rather than force.

The mystical reading works from the verbs of transfer. In {{5.0}} you roll your way off yourself, and the sentence that follows has no object at all: He will act, and what He will do is not specified, because the point of the handover is that you stop holding the outcome. In {{3.6}} you are told to graze on faithfulness, which makes trust a food rather than an attitude, something consumed daily and never stored. Against this the wicked in verse 20 are the reverse image, substance turning into smoke, mass leaving without being handed to anyone. The land in the refrain is then read as the settled state itself, the condition of being placed rather than the acreage, and inheriting it is what happens to a person who has stopped burning.
